analytic.title: Thermal Extension of the Total Bandwidth Server

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A typical real-time application is composed of periodic tasks with hard deadline constraints. It must also service aperiodic tasks that are generated in response to external and internal events. In addition to application's timing constraints, it is important that the system never violates thermal constraint due to its increasingly adverse impact on the processing platform. In this work, we propose a scheme for servicing aperiodic tasks in thermally constrained hard real-time systems. We propose an algorithm, T2BS, which is a thermal extension of the Total Bandwidth Server [1]. We show that our algorithm is optimal in the sense that it meets periodic task timing constraints as well as system thermal constraints; and it supports the maximum rate of aperiodic arrivals. Through extensive simulations we demonstrate the validity of theoretical results and perform the response time analysis of aperiodic tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Several embedded applications are composed of tasks which must finish within a certain time-frame. These applications span various fields from automotive/control (aircraftcontrol), multimedia (video conferencing) to biomedical (pacemakers) applications. In many of these systems, adherence to deadlines of individual tasks is of critical importance and any failure in the system/missed deadlines can lead to catastrophic consequences. These critical systems are called hard realtime systems. Real-time systems have been an active area of research for more than three decades. However, most research work considers only the timing constraints of real-time tasks. With the progression in IC technology, there are several additional constraints/factors (power, temperature) which have to be considered to ensure failure free operation of real-time systems.

This work focuses on scheduling of real-time applications in thermally constrained systems. It is important to consider thermal constraints due to rapid and increasing rise in power densities of modern processing platforms. ITRS 2012 update shows nearly doubling of average power density from 0.55-0.7 W/mm 2 in 2011 to 1.2-1.35 W/mm 2 by 2024 [2]. Increasing power densities lead to increased operating temperatures and thermal hotspots; which can adversely affect device reliability and performance [3]. To counteract increase in temperature, dynamic thermal management schemes are typically used to limit the power consumption of computing systems [4]. They fundamentally rely on varying the speed of the processor based on the current thermal behaviour of the system. However, in real time systems, the deadline constraints make the situation more complicated; as a decrease in processing speed may lead to deadline misses. This work covers the scheduling of aperiodic tasks and hard deadline periodic tasks. Periodic tasks are activated after regular time intervals called periods. Aperiodic tasks are activated in response to external/internal events; and therefore, their arrival times are known only at run time. There are several algorithms in literature which work on scheduling this mixed task model. These include Total Bandwidth Server [1], Sporadic Server [5], Deferrable Server [6] etc. However, none of these schemes are thermal aware. Therefore, scheduling using these schemes can cause thermal violations. Ahmed et al. [7] present a scheme for scheduling aperiodic tasks in non-preemptive thermally constrained systems. However, the presented scheme is not optimal in terms of either response time or service rate of aperiodics. Ahn et al. [8] use reactive speed scaling and a server based scheme to schedule aperiodic tasks with identical period periodic tasks.

In this work, we propose a thermal extension of Total Bandwidth Server scheme called Thermally Constrained Total Bandwidth Server (T2BS). T2BS schedules all periodic/aperiodic tasks at set rates assuming a fluid system. It uses the concepts of Thermal Utilization [9] to set execution rates such that there are no periodic task deadline violations and no system thermal violations. The contributions of this paper and its distinguishing aspects are following: 1) We propose a scheme for scheduling soft aperiodic tasks in thermally constrained real-time systems with hard deadline periodic tasks.

2) We assume that tasks have power variations. This is in contrast to the existing works which conservatively assume that power consumption is only a function of processor speed [8]; and does not vary across different tasks.

3) Our scheme, T2BS, is optimal in the sense of being able to support highest rate of aperiodic arrivals. 4) T2BS does not rely on speed scaling. Therefore, it can also be applied to systems which are not DVFS capable, or where the speed change overhead is prohibitively high. This paper is organized as follows: Section II covers the system and task model used in this work. This is followed by a review of theoretical results for Thermal Utilization [9] in section III. The proposed T2BS scheduling scheme is presented in section IV along with theoretical results. Working of T2BS is illustrated using an example in section V. This is followed by results in section VI and conclusion II. SYSTEM AND TASK MODEL a) Processor Model: In this work, we consider a singlecore system. The power consumed by the processor has two components: (i) dynamic power due to computational activities of a task, and (ii) leakage power due to leakage currents. Leakage power is approximated as a linear function of temperature [10]. As a result, if task τ is executing at time t, then the total power consumption at time t is written as:
div.formula: P tot (t, Ψ(t)) = P τ + δΨ(t) + ρ, (1
div.p: where P τ is the dynamic power due to computational activities of task τ , Ψ(t) is the processor temperature at time t and ρ and δ are modelling constants. The speed of the processor is assumed to be fixed. The processor temperature is required to remain below a threshold temperature Δ for safe operation. Hence, Δ is the thermal constraint of the processor.
b) Thermal Model: We use Fourier model to model thermal behaviour of the processor [9]. In this model, temperature of thermal elements is computed using following equation:
div.formula: C Ψ(t) = P (t) -AΨ(t),(2)
div.p: where C represents thermal capacitances, Ψ(t) is the temperature at time t, P (t) represents power consumption at time t. All of these symbols represent vectors with number of elements equal to the number of discrete thermal elements. A is a matrix, constructed using the thermal conductances between thermal elements. In the context of this paper, only one element of vector P (t) can have non-zero value (Representing the power consumption of the processor). The remaining elements will always be zero (Representing power consumption of passive thermal elements such as heat-spreader, heatsink etc). Following a few algebraic simplifications, similar to the ones performed in [9], we can simplify Equation 2:
div.formula: C Θ(t) = P dyn (t) -(A -δI)Θ(t). (3
div.p: where P dyn (t) represents the dynamic power consumption of the processor at time t, Θ(t) = Ψ(t) -Ψ idle,ss and Ψ idle,ss denotes a vector of steady state temperatures when the processor is idle (It only consumes leakage/static power). For simplicity of presentation, the rest of this paper assumes that all temperatures are expressed relative to the idle steady-state temperatures unless specified otherwise. The thermal constraint of the processor relative to steady-state temperature is Δ such that:Δ = Δ -Ψ idle,ss c) Task Model: The real-time application consists of periodic and aperiodic tasks. Let Γ denote the set of periodic tasks in the application. Each task τ ∈ Γ is characterized by: (i) worst-case computation time C τ , (ii) period T τ , and (iii) worst-case dynamic power consumption P τ . Furthermore, all tasks are assumed to be in-phase (Deadlines of all tasks are coincident with the end of their periods). Schedule of periodic tasks is represented as Π. The value of Π(t) represents a tuple with elements representing the task being executed at time t. The length of schedule Π is one hyperperiod (L); where hyperperiod is defined as the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the periods of all periodic tasks in Γ.

Aperiodic tasks do not conform to any specific arrival pattern and are not deadline constrained. An aperiodic task j is characterized by (i) release time R j , (ii) worst-case computation time C j , worst-case dynamic power consumption P j . It is assumed that these parameters are known when an aperiodic task arrives on the system. Note that both periodic and aperiodic tasks can have different dynamic power consumptions. This is a less restrictive model compared to most other works in real-time systems; which consider power consumption to be only a function of processor speed.

div.head: III. THEORETICAL REVIEW
div.p: In this section we first review the concepts of Total Thermal Impact and Thermal Utilization [9]. We then review the Total Bandwidth Server scheme [1] for scheduling aperiodic tasks.

div.head: B. Total Bandwidth Server (TBS)
div.p: TBS is a scheme for scheduling aperiodic tasks with hard deadline periodic tasks. The functioning of TBS is simple. When j th aperiodic task arrives at time R j with computation requirement C j , it is assigned a deadline D j such that:
div.formula: D j = max(R j , D j-1 ) + C j /U A
div.p: where D j-1 is the deadline assigned to the previous aperiodic task and U A is the computation utilization/system bandwidth assigned for the scheduling of aperiodic tasks. Once deadline (D j ) is assigned, TBS uses Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm to schedule periodic and aperiodic tasks.

TBS scheme has the ability to strictly bound the amount of execution aperiodic tasks receive within any time interval. Consider a time interval [t 1 , t 2 ] and let C ape be the total amount of aperiodic task execution in this interval. In [1], Spuri et al. prove that C ape ≤ (t 2t 1 )U A . Furthermore, they prove that there will be no timing violations if U A + U P ≤ 1, where U P is the total utilization of all periodic tasks. To guarantee maximum service for aperiodic tasks and no deadline violations for periodic tasks, TBS therefore sets U A + U P = 1. However, TBS is not a thermal-aware scheduling scheme. Therefore, using TBS in a thermally-constrained system may lead to thermal violations. We will illustrate this in section V. In the following section, we propose a new algorithm inspired by TBS called Thermally Constrained Total Bandwidth Server (T2BS).

div.head: A. Discretized T2BS
div.p: Discretized T2BS (D-T2BS) is a variant of T2BS where Worst Case Fair Weighted Fair Queuing (WF2Q) [14] is used instead of GPS to schedule periodic and aperiodic tasks. WF2Q is a scheduling scheme which approximates GPS when the system is not fluid (processor is not infinitely preemptible). In the context of this work, WF2Q will assign each task τ a weight of Cτ Tτ . WF2Q makes scheduling decisions for contiguous time periods called Execution Intervals. On a unicore system, WF2Q yields a schedule which is P-fair [15]; i.e. the execution done for each periodic task will have an absolute difference of less than 1 Execution Interval from its execution in a GPS schedule [14] at all times. Therefore, D-T2BS scheduling scheme will not cause any deadline misses if computation utilization is ≤ 1. Furthermore, the absolute difference in response time of D-T2BS and T2BS is upper bounded by:
div.formula: |W j,T 2BS -W j,D-T 2BS | ≤ Execution Interval min(U C A , ΔU T A /(ζP j ))(12)
div.p: The discretization of fluid scheduling scheme leads to a temperature profile that oscillates around the temperature profile of the fluid scheduling scheme executing the same tasks. At different time instances the temperature may be higher or lower than the temperature of the fluid scheme. This variation is a decreasing function of scheduling interval length and power variation across periodic/aperiodic tasks. Temperature variance because of discretization is illustrated in the example covered in next section and visually shown in Figure 2.

div.head: VI. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we analyze the performance of T2BS and D-T2BS algorithms through a series of experiments/simulations. We show that the response time of the T2BS algorithm closely follows the theoretical value computed using Equation 10. Furthermore, we demonstrate through extensive simulations that T2BS never exceeds threshold temperature. The performance of D-T2BS is also compared against T2BS.

Simulation Setup: We use the same thermal model as used in the example section (Section V). In our experiments U C P = 0.6 and U T P = 0.65. Therefore, U C A = 0.4 and U T A = 0.35. Aperiodic arrivals follow a Poisson process. In this section J will be used to to represent the set of all aperiodic tasks. For succinctness, we define power consumption
div.formula: P S = U T A Δ ζU C A = 84.92W
div.p: . Given an aperiodic task j; if P j > P S , then D j = D T j ; otherwise D j = D C j . P S will be used for explanation of results in this section. Without loss of generality, the computation time of all aperiodic tasks is assumed to be 100ms. For all simulations conducted, simulation points where aperiodic task utilization U A = λE(S) < 0.98 are simulated. As explained in section IV, U A ≥ 1 leads to an unstable system where aperiodic task response times grow unbounded.

Simulation Results: In the first experiment, we analyze the effect of aperiodic task power consumption and arrival rate on response time. In this experiment, aperiodic tasks are chosen from a set of aperiodic task types; with each type having different power consumption. By varying the probabilities of selecting aperiodic task types, different average power levels of aperiodic tasks are simulated. Average power consumption is P S , 1.5 × P S and 2 × P S for Low, Medium and High power levels respectively. In this experiment, 100,000 aperiodic tasks are scheduled for each simulation point. Figure 3 shows the measured value of average response time for different average power levels and arrival rates. The vertical lines in Figure 3 indicate the maximum arrival rate which can be supported for a given average power consumption, determined using Equation 11. Figure 3 also shows the analytical value of average response time which was determined using Equation 10. As shown in the figure, the response time of aperiodic tasks increases with an increase in arrival rate. Furthermore, response time also increases with an increase in average power consumption of aperiodic tasks. This is because aperiodic tasks with high power consumption are assigned larger deadlines. This increases the service time of aperiodic tasks; leading to an increase in response time. For all simulations conducted, the measured value of average response time matches very closely to the theoretical value from Equation 10.

In the next experiment, we conduct extensive simulations with 100 different arrival rates (λ) and 90 aperiodic task power consumptions (P ). Each distinct (λ, P ) pair constitutes a single simulation point in this experiment. For each simulation point, 100,000 aperiodic tasks are simulated with all of them having same power consumption. Figure 4 shows a heatmap, with color indicating response time. As shown in the figure, response time increases with an increase in arrival rate. An increase in power consumption does not cause an increase in response time when power consumption is less than P S . This is because D j = D C j when P j ≤ P S ; and power consumption has no effect on aperiodic task execution rate. When P j > P S , D j = D T j . Therefore, we see an increase in response time with an increase in power consumption > 84.9W . Figure 5 shows the maximum processor temperature for all simulation points. As shown in the figure, maximum temperature increases with an increase in aperiodic task power consumption <= P S . When aperiodic task power consumption is > P S , the maximum unadjusted temperature remains constant at 75 • C; since temperature is regulated by executing aperiodic tasks at lower rates based on their power consumption. Figure 4 Next, we compare the performance of D-T2BS with T2BS. The execution interval length for D-T2BS is 1ms. In this experiment we simulate 10,000 aperiodic tasks with power consumption equal to P S × 1.5 and λ = 2. Figure 6 shows the histogram of unadjusted temperature for T2BS and D-T2BS. As shown in the figure, T2BS and D-T2BS show similar temperature distribution. T2BS never exceeds threshold temperature. D-T2BS, however, has some thermal violations with maximum unadjusted temperature equal to (75.245 • C). This increase in temperature is due to discretization of the fluid T2BS schedule. div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This work presents an optimal scheme for scheduling a mix of periodic and aperiodic tasks in a thermally constrained system. We prove the optimality of proposed scheme (T2BS) in being able to support the maximum rate of aperiodic arrivals. The theoretical results are validated through extensive simulations. Several extensions to this work are possible and are part of on going research. The first of these extensions is formulation of thermal aware dynamic priority exchange algorithms. Dynamic priority exchange [1] is used to reduce response time (finish time) of aperiodic tasks. This involves exchange of priority/execution rate when there are no aperiodic tasks in the system and/or, when periodic/aperiodic tasks finish before their worst case computation time. Dynamic priority exchange algorithms will have to be modified to make them thermal aware. Another extension is the reduction of aperiodic task response time by taking advantage of temperature sensor readings. We can assign aperiodic tasks earlier thermal deadline if processor temperature is less than threshold. In such case, aperiodic tasks may finish earlier by algorithm T2BS. An extension of this work for muticore platforms is also part of future work.
